newsitem.title: USA: Judge approves historic Texaco settlement.
newsitem.headline: Judge approves historic Texaco settlement.

text.p: A federal judge has approved a historic discrimination suit settlement that rescues Texaco, Inc. from an ugly scandal involving tapes of executives making racist remarks and planning to destroy evidence.

Texaco's agreement to pay a record $176.1 million, the largest amount ever in such a suit, and to diversify its work force and business activities not only saved it from social disaster but won it praise from civil rights groups for creating a model to halt discrimination in the workplace.
U.S. District Judge Charles Brieant, in a ruling made available Wednesday, said he found the accord "fair and reasonable and highly beneficial to the class."

"That Texaco is sufficiently solvent to withstand a judgment beyond the dreams of avarice does not diminish in any way the extraordinary result for the class achieved by the settlement process," Brieant said in his order dated March 21.

Although the judge's approval marks the last hurdle for this class action, Texaco still faces other discrimination lawsuits, including a case filed last week by an engineer who alleges he was not hired because he is black.
The settlement approved by Brieant covers all blacks employed in salaried positions at Texaco or its subsidiaries at any time from March 23, 1991, through Nov. 15, 1996.

Although about 1,348 notices were sent to potential claimants, none chose to opt out of the plan and no objections were made during a fairness hearing held last week in White Plains, N.Y., federal court.

Brieant said since there are so many class members employed at different jobs and at various locations throughout the country, it would have been difficult for a jury to extrapolate evidence of apparent discrimination against one worker in one location and in one job title to apply to a national work force.
Plaintiffs' lawyers estimate that claimants will receive awards ranging from $60,000 to $80,000.

Brieant said he would rule later on fee applications by the two plaintiffs' firms that are seeking 25 percent of the cash part of the settlement. The judge said he had received letters from several claimants objecting to the requested fees, which would come to about $29 million.
The plan was well-received by civil rights groups and by the Rev. Jesse Jackson, who in December ended a consumer boycott of Texaco he helped initiate the previous month.

The NAACP Legal Defence and Educational Fund filed a brief supporting the settlement and told the court that the pact is "innovative and will be highly effective as a model for ending systemic discrimination in employment."

Texaco also reached an agreement with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission for the agency to intervene in the settlement. Under the accord, the EEOC will have rights to certain information, to monitor the settlement and to participate in court proceedings.

Although Texaco denies fault, it agreed on Nov. 15 to pay $176.1 million to settle the 1994 class-action lawsuit filed by black employees who alleged they were discriminated against in pay and promotions.

Separate from the settlement, Texaco also developed a plan to boost employment, career development and recruiting of minorities, as well as increasing purchasing from minority- and women-owned companies.

Texaco fired a top executive of an insurance subsidiary and took actions against other current and former employees who can be heard planning the destruction of documents on the tapes. The moves came after the company received a final report from an outside lawyer who investigated the situation.

The tapes were made public after Richard Lundwall, former senior coordinator of personnel services of Texaco's finance department, turned them over to the plaintiffs' lawyers. He and other executives can be heard on the tapes planning to destroy documents requested by the plaintiffs.
Although Lundwall turned over the tapes, he was subsequently indicted for obstruction of justice. He is the only defendant facing criminal charges growing out of the case.
